title: International Trade Reading List
text: This is a reading list mostly on classical trade theories, trade policy and some recent developments in the field within these sub fields. Generally, these topics are less interesting to the journals so there needs to be a newer empirical or theoretical hook for work on these models to continue. Or the more recent papers deal with contemporary questions and give answers to the discussion of our times.

title: International Trade Reading List
text:
Comparative Advantage

Pedagogic
Findlay, R. (1987). Comparative advantage. In The new Palgrave dictionary of economics (pp. 1-7). Palgrave Macmillan, London.
Bernhofen, D. M., & Brown, J. C. (2018). Retrospectives: On the genius behind David Ricardo’s 1817 formulation of comparative advantage. Journal of Economic Perspectives, 32(4), 227-240.


Theory
Dornbusch, R., Fischer, S., & Samuelson, P. A. (1977). Comparative advantage, trade, and payments in a Ricardian model with a continuum of goods. The American Economic Review, 67(5), 823-839. The definitive many good version of Ricardian model which has become the textbook version of Ricardian model at higher levels.
Costinot, A., Donaldson, D., Vogel, J., & Werning, I. (2015). Comparative advantage and optimal trade policy. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 130(2), 659-702.
This is a very important paper. The idea is that while we have a reasonable understanding of comparative advantage, we do not have an understanding of what this model says about trade policy and intervention. This is an attempt at answering different set of questions using the model which posits comparative advantage. * This is an interesting way of posing a question too. If we cannot contribute by asking old questions, ask new questions from the old model.

Gaubert, C., & Itskhoki, O. (2021). Granular comparative advantage. Journal of Political Economy, 129(3), 871-939. This is the most recent work using comparative advantage. This also could be the intersection of international trade (a conventional field) and industrial policy which specifically focuses on how to curb the market power of some large firms. They break down comparative advantage to an average firm behavior v. behavior generated by some large firms.
Grossman, G. M., & Helpman, E. (1990). Comparative Advantage and Long-Run Growth. The American Economic Review, 80(4), 796. Very well cited work.
Bernard, A. B., Redding, S. J., & Schott, P. K. (2007). Comparative advantage and heterogeneous firms. The Review of Economic Studies, 74(1), 31-66. Very well cited. The theory combines a two-country model with specialization based trade with heterogeneous firms.
Clarida, R. H., & Findlay, R. (1992). Government, trade, and comparative advantage. The American Economic Review, 82(2), 122-127. Intersection of comparative advantage and government intervention.
Costinot, A. (2009). An elementary theory of comparative advantage. Econometrica, 77(4), 1165-1192. Good extension of DFS.
Deardorff, A. V. (1980). The general validity of the law of comparative advantage. Journal of Political Economy, 88(5), 941-957.
Deardorff, A. V. (2005). How robust is comparative advantage?. Review of International Economics, 13(5), 1004-1016.
Costinot, A. (2009). On the origins of comparative advantage. Journal of International Economics, 77(2), 255-264.
Neary, J. P. (2007). Cross-border mergers as instruments of comparative advantage. The Review of Economic Studies, 74(4), 1229-1257.
Keesing, D. B. (1966). Labor skills and comparative advantage. The American Economic Review, 56(1/2), 249-258.
Redding, S. (1999). Dynamic comparative advantage and the welfare effects of trade. Oxford economic papers, 51(1), 15-39.
Matsuyama, K. (1992). Agricultural productivity, comparative advantage, and economic growth. Journal of economic theory, 58(2), 317-334.

title: International Trade Reading List
text:
Empirics

D. M. Bernhofen and J. C. Brown. A direct test of the theory of comparative advantage: the case of Japan. Journal of Political Economy, 112(1):48–67, 2004.
A. Costinot and D. Donaldson. Ricardo’s theory of comparative advantage: old idea, new evidence. American Economic Review Papers and Proceedings, 102(3):453–458, 2012.
Levchenko, A. A., & Zhang, J. (2016). The evolution of comparative advantage: Measurement and welfare implications. Journal of Monetary Economics, 78, 96-111. A sectoral take on specialization and comparative advantage. Cross country regressions but at the sectoral level. Thinking about doing this work, if it could be done, seems silly at this stage. Especially because at the time this work was published, cross country convergence regressions were discarded and empirical work would have been looked down upon.
Golub, S. S. and Hsieh, C.-T. (2000). Classical ricardian theory of comparative advantage revisited. Review of international economics, 8(2):221–234.
Chor, D. (2010). Unpacking sources of comparative advantage: A quantitative approach. Journal of International Economics, 82(2), 152-167.
Hummels, D. and Levinsohn, J. (1993). Product differentiation as a source of comparative advantage? The American Economic Review Papers and Proceedings, 83(2):445–449.
Hoen, A. R., & Oosterhaven, J. (2006). On the measurement of comparative advantage. The Annals of Regional Science, 40(3), 677-691.

title: International Trade Reading List
text:
Comparative Advantage Applied Elsewhere

Boehm, J., Dhingra, S., & Morrow, J. (2022). The comparative advantage of firms. Journal of Political Economy, 130(12), 3025-3100. Interesting piece of evidence on Indian firms production structure. The idea is that if firms have readily available inputs, then they tend to specialize and produce in the sector which has fewer input frictions.
Davis, D. R., & Dingel, J. I. (2020). The comparative advantage of cities. Journal of International Economics, 123, 103291. The idea is that of underlying labor specialization which causes some cities to specialize in some products. The intersection of labor and trade is very nice.
Hunt, S. D., & Morgan, R. M. (1995). The comparative advantage theory of competition. Journal of marketing, 59(2), 1-15. This piece is even more cited than the benchmark comparative advantage work by DFS. It is applying comparative advantage as a concept to marketing and explaining the monopoly power of firms. 5K citations and counting.
Suri, T. (2011). Selection and comparative advantage in technology adoption. Econometrica, 79(1), 159-209. This is the concept adapted to technology adoption by farmers. The data applied to an econometric model is what makes this work worthy of econometrica. It is a sharp neat application.
Nunn, N., & Trefler, D. (2014). Domestic institutions as a source of comparative advantage. Handbook of international economics, 4, 263-315. This paper examines how domestic institutions can be a source of comparative advantage. So rather than pinning comparative advantage to technology or labor productivity, this talks about institutions such as what Adam Smith mentions when he talks about institutions supporting free market to function and trade to occur.
Liu, X., Mattoo, A., Wang, Z., & Wei, S. J. (2020). Services development and comparative advantage in manufacturing. Journal of Development Economics, 144, 102438.
Do, Q. T., Levchenko, A. A., & Raddatz, C. (2016). Comparative advantage, international trade, and fertility. Journal of Development economics, 119, 48-66.
Ju, J., & Wei, S. J. (2011). When is quality of financial system a source of comparative advantage?. Journal of International Economics, 84(2), 178-187.

title: International Trade Reading List
text:
Purchasing Power Parity
The idea here is that purchasing power parity is a long run phenomenon with a convergence to this anchor in the very long run. Rogoff gives the 3-5 year half life result. Since the convergence is so slow, people are less interested in this theoretical long term benchmark but rather interested in short run exchange rate movements.
A leading reason for this lack of interest is: rather than viewing exchange rate parity as a result of equalization of goods prices, it started being viewed as a result of financial interaction, at least in the short run. This implies that things such as monetary policy differences across countries, capital flows, international exchange rate futures trade became more important to the determination of exchange rate.
A second reason for the disconnect is that firms price discriminate across countries which implies that exchange rate pass-through is incomplete and local currency pricing matters. Hence if by construction firms are treating different international markets differently, then the difference in exchange rate will reflect the difference in import/domestic consumption composition.
A third reason for the disconnect is that a large part of domestic prices is explained by non-tradables such as rents, local services such as haircuts, restaurants etc. Hence, when the CPI has more non-tradables, there is no reason to assume PPP equalization. This is connected to the idea extended by Balassa-Samuelson when they argued that countries will differ in price levels because of differences in productivity across tradeables which permeate into non-tradables.

Rogoff, K. (1996). The purchasing power parity puzzle. Journal of Economic literature, 34(2), 647-668.
Balassa, B. (1964). The purchasing-power parity doctrine: a reappraisal. Journal of political Economy, 72(6), 584-596.
Pinkovskiy, M., & Sala-i-Martin, X. (2020). Shining a light on purchasing power parities. American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics, 12(4), 71-108.
Taylor, A. M., & Taylor, M. P. (2002). The purchasing power parity debate. Journal of economic perspectives, 18(4), 135-158.
Dornbusch, R. (1987). Purchasing power parity. In The new Palgrave dictionary of economics (pp. 1-16). Palgrave Macmillan, London.
Vo, H. L., & Vo, D. H. (2023). The purchasing power parity and exchange‐rate economics half a century on. Journal of Economic Surveys, 37(2), 446-479.
Frenkel, J. A. (1978). Purchasing power parity: Doctrinal perspective and evidence from the 1920s. Journal of International Economics, 8(2), 169-191.

title: Introduction to Macroeconomics
text:
Why study it?

Things happening in the economy affect us significantly. Our career choices are an important result of the times we live in. See this Guardian article on Nascent tech, real fear: how AI anxiety is upending career ambitions.
Compulsary course?
Address questions such as

GDP: Why do some economies grow faster than others?

More capital resources
More labor/population resources
More productivity i.e. better and more efficient use of resources.

What is productivity? \(Y/L\) or the average output per worker employed in an economy or the average productivity of labor.


Unemployment: Why is there unemployment in these economies?
Inflation: Are rising
prices indicative of a supply shortage or a temporary excess demand?
Macroeconomic policy: Can economic policy control unanticipated movements in GDP?
International trade linkages: Does it help to trade with other economies or does it cause unwanted fluctuations in economic activity

title: Introduction to Macroeconomics
text:
Measurement in GDP

Growth rate. Here we consider time to progress from \(\ldots,t-2,t-1,t, t+1, t+2, \ldots\). We also consider this variable as discrete i.e. something that takes discontinuous but even steps. The “rate” refers to the fact that it is comparing today \(x_t\) to yesterday \(x_{t-1}\). If you think of absolute levels, then \(x_t\) levels i.e. say GDP levels do not make much sense. For eg: Australia’s GDP is 758337 mn = $758,337,000,000 or 758 billion, 337 million.1
\[g_x = \frac{x_t - x_{t-1}}{x_{t-1}}\]
There is so much more to growth rate that this formula, but the essential thing to think about is that it is calculating growth over a base i.e. comparing two time periods.

title: Online Readings for Introduction to Macroeconomics
text:
Why do I have this page?
I refer to some readings to introduce basic topics to undergraduates. This is a list of readings that I have referred to replaced and updated over the years. Some old ones are still very nice because they give a good introduction to the topic.


Labor Markets
These are the most recent readings which (a) introduce issues and (b) examine key debates in the labor market. I have updated this list over the years, and I think these are the best readings to introduce the topic to undergraduates.

Autor (2015)
Autor, David H. 2015. “Why Are There Still So Many Jobs? The History and Future of Workplace Automation.” Journal of Economic Perspectives 29 (3): 3–30.
Berger et al. (2026)
Berger, D., Herkenhoff, K., & Mongey, S. (2026). Labor Market Power: From Micro Evidence to Macro Consequences. Journal of Economic Perspectives, 40(1), 93-114.
Peri (2016)
Peri, G. (2016). Immigrants, productivity, and labor markets. Journal of economic perspectives, 30(4), 3-30.
Manning (2021)
Manning, A. (2021). The elusive employment effect of the minimum wage. Journal of Economic Perspectives, 35(1), 3-26.

Older versions of this list are still very good, and I have kept them here for reference.:

Autor, D. H. (2001). Wiring the labor market. Journal of Economic Perspectives, 15(1), 25-40.

I like this paper for its discussion of the labor market and how technology is changing it. It is a good introduction to the topic and provides a lot of insights into the future of work.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
section: Prologue: The Rise of Data Releases in Macroeconomics
text:
Prologue: The Rise of Data Releases in Macroeconomics
Macroeconomics has increasingly become a “high-frequency” discipline. Financial markets, central banks, journalists, and economists now react almost immediately to incoming economic data. Certain statistics — especially in the United States — have become highly influential because they provide rapid signals about inflation, employment, growth, and monetary policy.
The growing popularity of these data releases reflects three developments:

Central banks (especially the Federal Reserve) have become more data-dependent.
Financial markets respond aggressively to macroeconomic news surprises.
Media and public interest in inflation, recessions, and interest rates increased sharply after the Global Financial Crisis and especially after the COVID-19 inflation episode of 2021–23.

Below are some of the most closely watched macroeconomic indicators in modern macroeconomics.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Release Window

Released monthly
Usually the first Friday of every month
Published by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS)

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
What It Measures

Employment growth
Unemployment rate
Wage growth
Labor force participation

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Why It Became Popular
The jobs report became central because the Federal Reserve increasingly emphasized “maximum employment” as part of its dual mandate. After the 2008 financial crisis and again after COVID-19, labor market conditions became the main guide for monetary policy decisions.
Financial markets also realized that labor market tightness strongly predicts future inflationary pressure through wage growth.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Benefits of Tracking It
Economists use it to: - Gauge recession risk - Measure labor market tightness - Infer inflationary pressures - Predict Federal Reserve policy decisions - Assess household income growth and consumption strength

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Main Weakness
The report is volatile and subject to revisions.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Release Window

Released monthly
Usually around the middle of the month
Published by the BLS

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
What It Measures

Inflation faced by households
Prices of goods and services

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Why It Became Popular
Inflation was relatively stable from the mid-1990s to around 2020, so CPI attracted less public attention during the “Great Moderation.” However, the post-pandemic inflation surge made CPI one of the most watched statistics globally.
Markets now react intensely to “inflation surprises” because they alter expectations of future interest rates.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Benefits of Tracking It
Economists use CPI to: - Measure inflation persistence - Study real wage growth - Estimate cost-of-living changes - Forecast monetary policy tightening or easing

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Main Weakness
Headline CPI can be heavily influenced by volatile food and energy prices.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Release Window

Released monthly
Published by the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA)

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
What It Measures

Inflation excluding food and energy
Personal consumption expenditures price index

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Why It Became Popular
The Federal Reserve officially prefers Core PCE over CPI because: - It better captures substitution behavior - It has broader expenditure coverage - It is viewed as a cleaner measure of underlying inflation trends
As Fed communication became more transparent, economists increasingly focused on whichever inflation measure the Fed itself emphasized.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Benefits of Tracking It
Useful for: - Understanding trend inflation - Predicting Fed behavior - Filtering temporary price shocks

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Main Weakness
Less intuitive for the general public than CPI.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Release Window

Eight scheduled meetings per year
Announced by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC)

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
What It Measures

The Federal Reserve’s policy interest rate

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Why It Became Popular
Modern macroeconomics increasingly views monetary policy as the central stabilization tool of the economy. Since financial markets price assets based on expected future interest rates, every Fed decision has major implications for: - Bonds - Equity markets - Exchange rates - Housing markets
Fed communication itself has become an economic event.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Benefits of Tracking It
Economists use it to: - Infer the stance of monetary policy - Estimate recession probabilities - Understand financial conditions - Study transmission of monetary shocks

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Main Weakness
Markets often care more about future guidance than the current rate itself.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Release Window

Quarterly
Advance estimate released roughly one month after quarter end
Published by the BEA

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
What It Measures

Total output of the economy

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Why It Became Popular
GDP remains the broadest measure of aggregate economic activity and is still the standard measure of economic growth.
However, because GDP is released with delays, markets increasingly rely on “nowcasting” using higher-frequency indicators.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Benefits of Tracking It
Useful for: - Dating recessions - Measuring economic growth - Cross-country comparisons - Productivity analysis

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Main Weakness
Released slowly and heavily revised later.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Release Window

Weekly
Released every Thursday

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
What It Measures

Number of people filing unemployment insurance claims

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Why It Became Popular
Economists increasingly value high-frequency data because it gives faster information than monthly or quarterly releases. Initial claims became especially important during crises such as: - 2008 financial crisis - COVID-19 recession
It provides one of the fastest signals of labor market deterioration.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Benefits of Tracking It
Useful for: - Detecting turning points - Monitoring recession risk in real time - Measuring layoffs

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Main Weakness
Very noisy week-to-week.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Release Window

Continuously available in financial markets

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely

What It Measures

Difference between long-term and short-term interest rates

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Why It Became Popular
Yield curve inversion became famous because it historically predicted many U.S. recessions.
Modern macroeconomics increasingly incorporates financial markets into business cycle analysis, making bond market indicators highly influential.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Benefits of Tracking It
Useful for: - Predicting recessions - Understanding market expectations - Measuring expected future monetary policy

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely

Structural changes in bond markets may weaken predictive power.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely

Monthly
Released very early each month

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely

Business sentiment
Manufacturing and services activity

Markets value PMI because it arrives earlier than most “hard” economic data. It acts as an early indicator of: - Production - Demand - Employment intentions

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely

Because housing often turns before the broader economy, economists use it as a leading indicator.

title: Economics of Growth: Thoughts on the Evolution of the Literature
text: This is a reading list which dwells on the topic of economic growth. I have been reading a lot on this topic, and I find it very interesting. And if, as is often mentioned, traditional growth theory is dead, then what is the new turn?

title: Fiscal Policy via Public Finance
text:
What Fiscal Policy?
Fiscal policy has gone through popularity cycles based on discourse in academia. However, as many have argued (see Blinder), these cycles are more prominent in academic circles and less prominent in policy circles. Economic policy discussions have historically always included fiscal policy as a central theme, guiding such management throughout the broader arc of documented economic history. The last twenty years have seen a re-discussion of its place and a re-design of the economic thinking around fiscal policy with more evidence mounting towards its efficacy especially in times of limited maneuverability of monetary policy.
On this paper, I focus on the key aspects of fiscal policy, which are still contentious, need further empirical validation, and present an increasingly complicated fiscal ecosystem. This is also a reflection of the state and role of fiscal policy in the larger thinking in academic macroeconomics.

title: Fiscal Policy via Public Finance
text:
The Original Proposition
The debate surrounding the role of government came about historically. Between the two world wars and immediately after it, there were two strong forces which dictated the economic revival. There was a part of discourse which urged a hands off approach for the government and believed in private unfettered entrepreneurship driven by incentives and liberal choices. At the backdrop of the world war where choices were limited and individuals were restricted, economies were constrained, this was a counter-movement to the global political order. On the other end of the spectrum was this realization that governments must lead the revival of economies with large public spending programs and greater interactions with markets in most economies. The extreme position was one where governments were the only method of resource allocation and economic prosperity. Hence there was a historical re-thinking of the role of government intervention in an economy at the same time there was a general shift in the way the world works.

text:
Market Faliures
Those who argued the general absence of government also conceded the need to facilitate government intervention in cases where market system collapses for some reason.

text:
Role of Sovereign
``The operation of the public sector, as developed by the classical economists, is seen in the context of a natural order which calls for reliance on and non-interference with the market…The prince, therefore, is “discharged from any duty of superintending the industry of private people”. But the system of natural liberty still needs the prince. It requires him to perform three duties, “duties of great importance indeed, but plain and intelligible to common understandings”. These duties are, first, to protect society against invasion from abroad; second, to protect every member of society from the injustice of every other member; and third, to provide certain institutions and public works…’’

Normative vs Positive

title: Fiscal Policy via Public Finance
section: How economists think about fiscal policy
text:
How economists think about fiscal policy
In 2000, a survey of 298 members of the American Economic Association (AEA) found that while 84 percent generally agreed with the statement “Fiscal policy has a significant stimulative impact on a less than fully employed economy”, 71 percent also generally agreed with the statement “Management of the business cycle should be left to the Federal Reserve; activist fiscal policy should be avoided.”
In 2011, a follow-up survey of 568 AEA members found that the previous consensus about the latter proposition had dissolved and was by then roughly evenly disputed.

title: Fiscal Policy via Public Finance
section: Can we categorize fiscal policy as expansionary or contractionary?
text:
Can we categorize fiscal policy as expansionary or contractionary?
The idea is that since fiscal policy is linked to output i.e. proportional to output, we have an automatic increase and decrease of fiscal revenue and expenditure at least to the extent that they are proportional to output.
However, these definitions can be misleading because, even with no changes in spending or tax laws at all, cyclic fluctuations of the economy cause cyclic fluctuations of tax revenues and of some types of government spending, altering the deficit situation; these are not considered to be policy changes. Therefore, for purposes of the above definitions, “government spending” and “tax revenue” are normally replaced by “cyclically adjusted government spending” and “cyclically adjusted tax revenue”. Thus, for example, a government budget that is balanced over the course of the business cycle is considered to represent a neutral and effective fiscal policy stance.

title: Fiscal Policy via Public Finance
section: Financing with Bonds/Debt and its International Implications
text:
Financing with Bonds/Debt and its International Implications
When governments fund a deficit with the issuing of government bonds, interest rates can increase across the market, because government borrowing creates higher demand for credit in the financial markets. This decreases aggregate demand for goods and services, either partially or entirely offsetting the direct expansionary impact of the deficit spending, thus diminishing or eliminating the achievement of the objective of a fiscal stimulus.
In the classical view, expansionary fiscal policy also decreases net exports, which has a mitigating effect on national output and income. When government borrowing increases interest rates it attracts foreign capital from foreign investors. This is because, all other things being equal, the bonds issued from a country executing expansionary fiscal policy now offer a higher rate of return. In other words, companies wanting to finance projects must compete with their government for capital so they offer higher rates of return. To purchase bonds originating from a certain country, foreign investors must obtain that country’s currency. Therefore, when foreign capital flows into the country undergoing fiscal expansion, demand for that country’s currency increases. The increased demand, in turn, causes the currency to appreciate, reducing the cost of imports and making exports from that country more expensive to foreigners. Consequently, exports decrease and imports increase, reducing demand from net exports.

title: Monetary Policy and the Phillips Curve
text:
A model of monetary policy is trying to establish a gap between where we desire the economy to reach and where it currently stands. This takes the form of two specific targets (a) an inflation gap and and (b) output gap.
The inflation gap refers to the deviation of the current inflation rate \(\pi_t\) from a desired target level \(\pi_t^*\). When such a deviation exists, it provides the rationale for monetary policy intervention.
The determination of the target \(\pi^*_t\) itself raises a deeper question: what principle governs its selection? The historical and theoretical justifications for a specific inflation target are not unambiguous; however, a broad consensus has emerged that price stability — typically associated with low and stable inflation — is a prerequisite for sustainable economic growth. A widely held aversion to high inflation reflects concerns about its distortionary effects on resource allocation, income distribution, and long-run economic performance. This is partly the recent history of high inflation after the oil price shocks which left a painful memory in the politics of US that Fed and other central bankers have become more Hawkish.
The output gap refers to the deviation of current output from a notion of potential output. While the concept of an inflation target is a question of acceptable levels of inflation, the discussion surrounding potential output is equally difficult to approach. It is that level of output at which our resources are completely employed, we are at our capacities and there is no slack in the economy. This implies an underlying knowledge of efficiency and use of resources. This also implies that we assume full employment is the sense of potential. In the world of AI, perhaps this might change and economists might include a participation dimension into this equation. However, as it stands, we have this notion of capacity which we aspire to attain an an economy which defines our “potential”.
Once we construct these measures of gap, one needs one more validity for monetary intervention. That is the idea that this gap will not be filled automatically, hence there is a need for intervention. Or that this gap may be filled automatically, but intervention will accelerate this process. The standard argument for existence of a gap is a temporary excess supply or demand which eventually will settle down based off price signals. The mechanism of the market will incentivise necessary adjustments. However, the intervention implies that the rate at which market responds will cause a lot of pain to people and as policy makers, by intervening in this market we could improve the speed of adjustment.
A stronger justification for intervention arises in models where the economy may not naturally converge back to equilibrium, or where disequilibrium can persist for extended periods. Such ideas appear in disequilibrium macroeconomics and non-Walrasian models associated with economists such as Clower, Leijonhufvud, Malinvaud, and Barro–Grossman Barro and Grossman (1971) . In these frameworks, prices may adjust slowly, quantity constraints may bind, and market outcomes need not automatically generate forces sufficient to restore equilibrium. These approaches are less common in modern macroeconomics, partly because contemporary rational expectations models typically eliminate explosive or non-convergent paths through equilibrium selection conditions.

title: Monetary Policy and the Phillips Curve
text:
Monetary Models
In most models of monetary policy, we essentially have 3 things. First, a version of the dynamic IS curve which implements the dynamism of modern macro-models through the Euler equation. Second, a version of the Phillips curve which professes that in the short run there is a tradeoff between inflation and unemployment. Since the unemployment can be mapped directly to output via an aggregate production function, we think of this trade off as one between output and inflation. Third, we have the rule which defines how monetary policy intervenes in this market, if it can intervene in a stable manner.

title: Monetary Policy and the Phillips Curve
text:
Phillips Curve
The key issue in the business cycle literature is the existence of Phillips curve. The first thread was establishment of this inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation.
Phillips, A. W. (1958). The relation between unemployment and the rate of change of money wage rates in the united kingdom, 1861–1957 1. Economica, 25(100):283–299. Phillips (1958)
This is the seminal paper in this literature. The paper documents a negative relationship between unemployment and wage inflation in the UK. Originally, it talked about money wage i.e. nominal wages rate changes affecting unemployment level and unemployment rate. He concludes with this statement “These conclusions are of course tentative. There is need for much more detailed research into the relations between unemployment, wage rates, prices and productivity.”
He begins with the idea that if net demand is positive, it leads to price rise. Similarly he says the same thing should happen to money wages. If there is excess demand, money wages should rise. “When the demand for labour is high and there are very few unemployed we should expect employers to bid wage rates up quite rapidly, each firm and each industry being continually tempted to offer a little above the prevailing rates to attract the most suitable labour from other firms and industries.”

title: Monetary Policy and the Phillips Curve
text:
Implications from the Phillips Curve
The consequence of this study was that governments could pick and choose a point on the Phillips curve. In the short run they could use monetary and fiscal policy to increase demand, reduce unemployment and track the relative increase in inflation along the curve.
However, Friedman (1968) and Phelps (1967) argued that this inverse relationship needs context. The idea is that expansionary policy can temporarily push unemployment below its natural rate because wages and prices do not adjust immediately. But once workers and firms revise their inflation expectations, real wages and relative prices adjust, and unemployment returns to its natural rate. The long-run result is simply higher inflation, not permanently lower unemployment. So the policy option which appears in the short run is actually not a permanent fix.
Friedman (1968)
Monetary policy has powerful short-run effects but limited long-run effects. He puts the discussion of the trade-off between inflation and unemployment in the context of expectations. He argues that in the long run, the Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment, and that any attempt to keep unemployment below this natural rate will lead to accelerating inflation. So while this is a statement of what monetary policy can and cannot do, it is also a statement about the nature of the Phillips curve and the trade-off between inflation and unemployment.
Phelps (1967)
Phelps’ interpretation is that \(u^*\) is the unemployment rate consistent with correctly anticipated inflation. Attempts to keep unemployment below \(u^*\) require continually accelerating inflation. To keep unemployment permanently below the natural rate, policymakers would need to generate ever-increasing inflation surprises.

title: Monetary Policy and the Phillips Curve
text:
Microfounding the Expectations Argument
While Phelps and Friedman argued that the economy will return to this natural rate in the long run, their argument was that interventions are limited and crucially depend on how expectations react to shocks and to policy. This was microfounded in the Rational expectations model by Lucas Jr (1972)
Lucas Jr (1972)
The Phillips curve is not stable and can shift due to changes in expectations. He argues that in the long run, there is no trade-off between inflation and unemployment. He introduces the concept of rational expectations and argues that if people have rational expectations, then any attempt to exploit the Phillips curve will be futile because people will anticipate the effects of monetary policy and adjust their behavior accordingly.
Lucas and Rapping (1969)
Lucas–Rapping asked: Through what optimizing behavior do expectations affect employment? Their answer: Workers move labor across time in response to perceived real wage changes. This was one of the first attempts to make the Phillips curve consistent with an optimization, idea of expectations, and an equilibrium reasoning. It is not yet the fully developed rational-expectations model of Lucas (1972), but it is a major step toward it. Since it is a developing answer one which was taken to the next level by Lucas (1972), it is not as well-known as the later paper, but it is an important step in the development of the literature.
Lucas Jr (1976)
Made a similar claim stating that when policy makers react, then agents adjust their expectations and there could be a regime shift. Think along the lines of Friedman and Phelps but micro-founding the expectations argument.

title: Monetary Policy and the Phillips Curve
text:
Rules v. Discretion
So the argument that is being extended here is that central banks cannot do anything because agents will anticipate their behavior, adjust and we will switch regimes instantly. This is where the argument was extended that discretionary policy may be ineffective by Sargent and Wallace (1975). Their key point is that if people understand the monetary policy rule and form expectations rationally, then systematic monetary policy cannot systematically fool people, so anticipated monetary policy has little or no effect on real variables like output or unemployment. This is closely tied to the Phillips curve debate because it attacks the idea that policymakers can repeatedly exploit inflation surprises.
This then led policy makers to ask, what should central banks do? How should monetary policy be conducted keeping in mind this argument that you cannot systematically fool people. So if the central bank is setting a policy which is discretionary, agents will observe this behavior and adjust their expectations from the central bank. That could defeat the solution proposed by monetary policy in the first place and render monetary policy ineffective.
The solution was to generate perpetual monetary policy shocks. Could this be done? Perhaps yes, but not with ill effects.
The alternative was to provide a rule based policy Kydland and Prescott (1977) and Taylor (1993)
The key insight is that discretionary policymakers have an incentive to create surprise inflation to temporarily boost output, but rational agents anticipate this. The result is an inflation bias with little long-run gain in employment or output. Rules or credible commitments are proposed as a solution to this credibility problem.

title: Monetary Policy and the Phillips Curve
section: Did this debate lock us out?
text:
Did this debate lock us out?
While Friedman, Phelps and Lucas made strong arguments which had expectations at their core, the empirical observation by Phillips still needed explanation. Was it the persistence of regimes which caused an expost observation of inverse inflation and unemployment relationship? Was it temporary? Why do monetary and demand shocks have real effects at all if agents are rational and markets clear continuously? Without stickiness or information frictions, rational expectations models implied very limited real effects of anticipated policy. That made it difficult to explain recessions, persistent unemployment, large output fluctuations, and the observed effects of monetary policy.
So we were stuck. We said policy cannot exploit this. Let us set a rule. Once we set a rule, even then these shocks which keep hitting the economy have real effects which shift unemployment above or below its natural rate. Can central bank not do anything after setting the rule here? Did we just play ourselves into a corner?
